state.misconception_label: Has used slant height and base to find area of a triangle rather than perpendicular height and base

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: How would you calculate the area of this triangle? ![A triangle, base 12m. All three sides are equal.](). I got \( \frac{12 \times 12}{2} \) because I added the side lengths instead of multiplying.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have a tent with a slanted roof, and you want to find the area of the triangular section. To do this, you would need to measure the perpendicular height from the peak of the roof down to the base, not the slant height. In this case, we need to use the perpendicular height to calculate the area of the triangle.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so I need to measure straight down from the top to the base, not along the slanted side? But how do I actually find that perpendicular height if I'm only given the side lengths of the triangle?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you're building a pyramid out of blocks. To find the height of the pyramid, you would stack the blocks straight up from the base, not along the slanted sides. In the same way, to find the perpendicular height of a triangle, you need to draw a straight line from the top to the base, creating a right angle with the base. This perpendicular height is what you use to calculate the area of the triangle.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: So I need to draw a line straight down from the top vertex to the base at a right angle, and that's the height I use in the formula? But in this equilateral triangle problem, how do I actually work out what that perpendicular height is if I only know the sides are 12m?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses analogies to explain perpendicular height but never addresses the student's actual misconception (using slant height in the formula), doesn't teach how to find the perpendicular height when asked twice, and the student shows no progress toward solving the problem despite repeatedly asking the same question.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete real-world analogies (tent roof, pyramid blocks) to explain the abstract concept of perpendicular height, though they don't ultimately help the student solve the computational problem of finding the actual height value.
